summary:
HaloCrew is a calm, all-in-one health and wellbeing workspace designed for astronauts on long-duration missions. We developed a browser-based prototype with detailed hardware integration that brings together health monitoring, manual medical logging, wellbeing check-ins, mission records, crew and family connection, AI support, and interactive wearable concepts such as the Bio-Glove, Bio-Suit, and Vision-Guard.
It addresses the challenge of keeping astronauts healthy when they are far from immediate medical care by turning scattered readings and personal check-ins into clear, practical next steps. Rather than overwhelming users with data, Halo Crew helps them understand how they are doing today and maintain a useful record over time.
This matters because space travel is deeply human; physical health, mental wellbeing, connection, and confidence all affect mission success. In space far from our earth, the crews have only themselves to depend on, and Halo-Crew assists in to alleviate this load off of them as much as possible.
details:
HaloCrew is our response to a growing challenge in human spaceflight; as missions travel farther from Earth and last longer, astronauts will face greater health risks with less immediate access to medical support. The project is a browser-based health and wellbeing workspace that helps crew members check in with themselves, understand health information, and keep a record they can share with mission support.

The prototype brings health indicators, trends, status explanations, and sample alerts together in one place, such that our astronauts can enter readings such as blood pressure, blood glucose, or radiation dose, follow measurement guidance, and keep mission check-ins. Wellbeing tools, daily routines, crew and family connections, and an optional AI copilot recognize that isolation and confinement can affect mental health as much as physical health. The aim is to make useful information easier to understand and act on, so potential concerns can be noticed earlier and communicated clearly.

What makes HaloCrew distinctive is that it treats astronaut health as a whole- body, mind, routines, and relationships. Its interactive Halo-Suit Studio also presents concepts for future wearable tools, including the Bio-Glove, Bio-Suit, and Vision-Guard. These models help show how new sensor ideas might fit into a broader health system.

We built the software with React, TypeScript, and Three.js. , a Node.js backend supports mission records and storage, with optional PostgreSQL, AI, and voice services. Alongside, hardware concepts were developed with FreeCAD and include 3D models and design documentation.

With available data on NASA's research sites and with the help of implication of more relevant data from partnered organizations, we can aspire for more accurate and helpful outcome with our HaloCrew- as its personal trained LLM will have data with more personalization as well as accuracy on predicting and identifying our crews' states in the unpredictable environment of space.

Our team considered the realities of long missions- radiation, altered gravity, distance from Earth, isolation, limited access to care, and the need for astronauts to assess themselves. We also considered to cover clear visual design, simple instructions, data freshness, and ways to keep records useful to the crew and flight surgeons.

The urgency is real, on a distant mission, a small health concern may become harder to address if it goes unnoticed, and right there Halo-Crew pitches in as it explores how a calm, connected tool could help astronauts stay informed and supported. It is a demonstration prototype using mostly simulated data; it is not a validated medical device with greater potential to the extent our astronauts need in their missions, to take more giant leaps for mankind.
